bibl.title: Millisecond encoding precision of auditory cortex neurons
bibl.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether individual auditory cortex neurons carry stimulus information in spike times precise to a few milliseconds, and what feature of the spike train carries it
span.quote: One central question pertains to the relevance of millisecond-precise spike times of individual auditory cortical neurons for stimulus encoding.

span.label: how precisely must spike times be registered before stimulus information is lost
span.quote: We investigated the dependence of stimulus information on the temporal precision at which spike times were registered and found that registering spikes at a precision coarser than a few milliseconds significantly reduced the encoded information. This dependence demonstrates that auditory cortex neurons can carry stimulus information at high temporal precision.

span.label: shows that registering spikes coarser than a few milliseconds loses information, that the carrier is fast modulation of firing rate rather than spike-time correlations, and that the precision depends on the stimulus dynamics
span.quote: In addition, we found that the main determinant of finely timed information was rapid modulation of the firing rate, whereas higher-order correlations between spike times contributed negligibly.

span.label: existence
span.quote: This dependence demonstrates that auditory cortex neurons can carry stimulus information at high temporal precision.

span.label: millisecond spike-timing precision in auditory cortex
span.quote: One central question pertains to the relevance of millisecond-precise spike times of individual auditory cortical neurons for stimulus encoding.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We recorded single neurons’ responses in the caudal auditory cortex of passively listening macaque monkeys.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Faster stimulus dynamics drive more rapid membrane depolarizations, whose steeper threshold crossings produce more precisely timed spikes, which in turn carry stimulus information at finer temporal precision.
span.quote: On the basis of this hypothesis, our results suggest that stimuli with faster dynamics elicit more rapid membrane depolarizations and, hence, more precisely timed spikes that, in return, then encode stimulus information at high temporal precision.

span.label: effective precision is degraded by shuffling spikes between neighbouring bins, which lowers resolution without changing the statistical dimensionality of the data
span.quote: This shuffling procedure entailed shuffling spikes in nearby time bins (compare Methods and Fig. S2 A ) and can be used to progressively degrade the effective precision of a spike train without affecting the statistical dimensionality of the data.

span.label: direct mutual information is used instead of decoding precisely because a decoder can miss information a neuron actually carries
span.quote: We computed direct estimates of the mutual information between stimulus and neural response, which can capture all of the information that neural responses carry about the sound stimuli.

span.label: and the two are then run against each other on the same data, showing the method itself shifts the apparent coding timescale
span.quote: We found that linear decoding resulted in smaller losses of stimulus information when degrading temporal precision and, hence, would have indicated a coarser encoding time scale than that found with direct estimates of the stimulus information

span.label: the stimulus is chosen to make the test hardest - random chords have a correlation time of a few milliseconds and are the case where precise timing was argued not to survive
span.quote: Given that this stimulus has a short (few milliseconds) correlation time scale ( Fig. 1 B ), and given the debate about whether there could be a precise temporal encoding in the absence of response locking to fast sequences of stimulus presentations ( 7 ), random chords are particularly suited to determine whether precise spike timing can contribute to the encoding of complex sounds within a rich acoustic background.

span.label: a second stimulus class with a much slower correlation structure is run so that stimulus dynamics becomes a variable rather than a constant
span.quote: In a second experiment we further tested the importance of sampling responses at millisecond precision using an additional set of neurons ( n = 31) recorded during the presentation of natural sounds. This stimulus ( Fig. 2 A ), which has correlation time scale of few tens of milliseconds ( Fig. 2 B ), comprised a continuous sequence of environmental sounds, animal vocalizations and conspecific macaque vocalizations.

span.label: the peak-width measure is explicitly declared insufficient before the information analysis is introduced, because a spike could carry information by where it falls within a peak
span.quote: Yet, the width of PSTH peaks does not fully establish the temporal scale at which spikes carry information, because, for example, spikes might encode stimulus information depending on where they occur within a PSTH peak. We thus used Shannon information [ I ( S ; R ); Eq. 1 ] to directly quantify the information carried by temporal spike patterns sampled at different temporal precision.

span.label: the information estimate is built to assume nothing about which acoustic features drive the cell
span.quote: It is important to note that, in the formalism used here, the information theoretic calculation does not make assumptions about the particular acoustic features driving the responses (see also refs. 15 and 40 ). As a result, our information estimates the overall amount of knowledge about the sensory environment that can be gained from neural response.

span.label: significance of information loss is established per neuron against an artificial response carrying no information at that precision
span.quote: This bootstrap test demonstrated that the information loss was significant ( P < 0.05) for some neurons already at 4-ms effective precision (7% of the neurons), and for nearly half the neurons (46%) at 12-ms precision

span.label: the rate-versus-correlation question is settled by computing the information available to an observer who sees only the time-dependent rate
span.quote: It could be that the only information-bearing feature is the temporal modulation of the PSTH, hence the time-dependent firing rate. However, it could also be that higher-order correlations within the spike response pattern carry additional information.

span.label: the precision bound is bracketed from both sides rather than reported as a single figure
span.quote: In addition, we did not find neurons with a significant information loss when reducing the response precision from 1- to 2-ms bins. This result demonstrates that for the present dataset the temporal precision of information coding is coarser than one, but finer than ≈4–6 ms.

span.label: the discrepancy with earlier work is attributed to two separable method differences, and the experiment that would separate them is specified
span.quote: Future studies should directly investigate the context dependency of neural coding time scales, by e.g., presenting the same set of stimuli either separated by extended periods of silence or embedded in a context of stimuli of the same kind.

span.label: Because coding precision tracks stimulus dynamics, the reported precision is a lower bound and could be finer with faster stimuli.
span.note: what this limits: the precision figure, with its direction: OUR RESULTS MAY RATHER PROVIDE A LOWER BOUND ON THE EFFECTIVE PRECISION, LEAVING THE POSSIBILITY THAT AUDITORY CORTEX NEURONS MIGHT ENCODE SENSORY INFORMATION AT THE (SUB) MILLISECOND SCALE
span.quote: In light of this stimulus dependency, our results may rather provide a lower bound on the effective precision, leaving the possibility that auditory cortex neurons might encode sensory information at the (sub) millisecond scale.

span.label: The higher precision found here relative to earlier work may be an artefact of the continuous-sequence stimulation paradigm rather than a general property.
span.note: what this limits: the comparison with earlier reports, which is the paper's novelty: OUR FINDING OF A HIGHER CODING PRECISION THAN IN PREVIOUS STUDIES MIGHT WELL RESULT FROM THIS DIFFERENCE IN STIMULATION PARADIGM
span.quote: Our finding of a higher coding precision than in previous studies might well result from this difference in stimulation paradigm.

span.label: The context dependence of coding time scales was not directly tested and is left to future work.
span.note: what this limits: the generality of the time scales: FUTURE STUDIES SHOULD DIRECTLY INVESTIGATE THE CONTEXT DEPENDENCY OF NEURAL CODING TIME SCALES
span.quote: Future studies should directly investigate the context dependency of neural coding time scales, by e.g., presenting the same set of stimuli either separated by extended periods of silence or embedded in a context of stimuli of the same kind.

span.label: the precision reported is a lower bound, since faster stimuli might reveal finer coding
span.note: duplicate of: limitations[0] · what this limits: the same scope as item 0 - faster stimuli could reveal finer coding
span.quote: In light of this stimulus dependency, our results may rather provide a lower bound on the effective precision, leaving the possibility that auditory cortex neurons might encode sensory information at the (sub) millisecond scale.

span.label: coding precision was much more variable across neurons for natural sounds, and the population loss was smaller than for random chords
span.note: what this limits: the natural-sound results specifically: THE PROPORTIONAL INFORMATION LOST BY REDUCING THE EFFECTIVE TEMPORAL PRECISION WAS SMALLER THAN THE RESULTS OBTAINED DURING STIMULATION WITH RANDOM CHORDS
span.quote: In fact, across the entire sample of neurons, the proportional information lost by reducing the effective temporal precision was smaller than the results obtained during stimulation with random chords

span.label: the difference from previous reports may itself be an artefact of presenting sounds continuously rather than in isolation
span.note: duplicate of: limitations[1] · what this limits: the same scope as item 1 - continuous versus isolated presentation may explain the difference from previous work
span.quote: Our finding of a higher coding precision than in previous studies might well result from this difference in stimulation paradigm.

span.label: the biophysical account of why faster stimuli give more precise spikes is offered as a simple hypothesis
span.note: what this limits: the mechanistic account: A SIMPLE HYPOTHESIS IS THAT PRECISION OF SPIKE TIMES IS DETERMINED BY THE SLOPE OF THE MEMBRANE VOLTAGE WHEN CROSSING THE FIRING THRESHOLD - offered as a hypothesis, not shown
span.quote: A simple hypothesis is that precision of spike times is determined by the slope of the membrane voltage when crossing the firing threshold, with steeper slopes resulting in more precise spike times

span.label: the link to behaviour is explicitly a temptation rather than a result
span.note: what this limits: the link to behaviour: IT IS TEMPTING TO HYPOTHESIZE THAT SUCH MILLISECOND-PRECISE SINGLE NEURON-ENCODING SERVES AS NEURAL SUBSTRATE FOR RECENTLY REPORTED BEHAVIORAL CORRELATES
span.quote: It is tempting to hypothesize that such millisecond-precise single neuron-encoding serves as neural substrate for recently reported behavioral correlates of millisecond-precise cortical activity. For example, trained rats were shown to being able to report millisecond differences in patterns of electrical microstimulation applied to auditory cortex ( 31 ), demonstrating that auditory cortex can access temporally precise patterns of local activity.

span.label: Shannon's mutual information, defined over a set of stimuli and a set of responses, is imported as the direct measure of what a spike train tells an observer about the sound
span.quote: We thus used Shannon information [ I ( S ; R ); Eq. 1 ] to directly quantify the information carried by temporal spike patterns sampled at different temporal precision.

span.label: Shannon mutual information estimated directly, chosen because it bounds all the information a response could carry rather than what a particular decoder can extract
span.quote: Shannon information measures the reduction of uncertainty about the stimulus gained by observing a single trial response (averaged over all stimuli and responses) and was computed from many (average 55) repeats of the same stimulus sequence by using the direct method

span.label: the finding that response precision scales with stimulus speed, imported as the prediction that the auditory answer should depend on stimulus dynamics
span.quote: Our results reveal a dependency of neural response precision on the prominent stimulus time scales: The average PSTH-derived response precision ( Figs. 1 D and 2 D ) was finer, and the information loss with decreasing response precision ( Figs. 1 E and 2 E ) was larger, for the chord stimulus, which had a much shorter autocorrelation time scale than the natural sounds (compare Figs. 1 and 2 B ).

span.label: each stimulus repeated many times - 55 repeats on average, range 39 to 70
span.note: eliminates: a spike-timing precision estimate built on too few trials to separate reliable timing from chance alignment
span.quote: Each stimulus was repeated multiple times (on average 55 repeats of the same stimulus, range 39–70 repeats) and for a given recording site only one of the two stimuli was presented.

span.label: temporal coding - as spike-time correlations carrying information beyond the rate versus as fast modulation of the rate itself; the paper finds the second and so the dichotomy dissolves
span.quote: This high fraction demonstrates that essentially the entire stimulus information can be extracted without knowledge of higher-order correlations. Modulations of time-dependent firing rate are thus a key factor in the auditory cortical representation of sounds.

span.label: precision of the neural code - defined operationally as the coarsest resolution that still yields all the information a response carries
span.quote: Determining the precision of the neural code (i.e., the coarsest resolution sufficient to extract all of the information carried by a neuron's response) is a fundamental prerequisite for characterizing and understanding sensory representations

span.label: response precision - as PSTH peak width versus as information loss under degraded resolution; the first is declared insufficient and the second is what the claims rest on
span.quote: Yet, the width of PSTH peaks does not fully establish the temporal scale at which spikes carry information, because, for example, spikes might encode stimulus information depending on where they occur within a PSTH peak. We thus used Shannon information [ I ( S ; R ); Eq. 1 ] to directly quantify the information carried by temporal spike patterns sampled at different temporal precision.

span.label: coding timescale - as a property of the neuron versus as a property of the neuron given a stimulus; the same cells are more precise for faster sounds
span.quote: Our results hence suggest that the neural response precision and the importance of millisecond-precise spike patterns may depend on the overall dynamics of stimulus presentation.

span.label: millisecond precision - established at the auditory periphery and subcortex, but contested at cortex; the paper places cortex between the two
span.quote: In the auditory system, the role of millisecond-precise spike times is well established at the peripheral and subcortical level ( 29 , 30 ), but it remains debated whether auditory cortical neurons encode acoustic information with millisecond-precise spike timing

span.label: a sound presented in silence versus embedded in a continuous stream of similar sounds - two paradigms that may give different answers about the same neurons
span.quote: For example, previous studies reporting a 10- to 20-ms coarse coding precision of auditory cortex neurons were based on the presentation of short stimuli (natural sounds or clicks) interspersed with long periods of silence ( 9 , 11 ). In such paradigms, individual “target” sounds are presented in a context of silence. In contrast to such a paradigm, we here presented continuous sequences of sounds, hence effectively embedding each target sound in the context of other (similar) sounds.

span.label: claim_type: existence
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: existence — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Our results demonstrate that neurons in primate auditory cortex can indeed use spike times with a precision of a few milliseconds to carry information about complex and behaviorally relevant sounds, albeit at a precision coarser than found for peripheral or subcortical auditory structures.

span.label: method: single-unit recording in passively listening macaques during long continuous random-chord and natural-sound sequences, with direct Shannon information estimates and a spike-shuffling procedure that degrades effective precision
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: electrophysiology — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: This shuffling procedure entailed shuffling spikes in nearby time bins (compare Methods and Fig. S2 A ) and can be used to progressively degrade the effective precision of a spike train without affecting the statistical dimensionality of the data.

span.label: phenomenon: temporal precision of the neural code in auditory cortex
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: millisecond spike-timing precision in auditory cortex — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Neurons in auditory cortex are central to our perception of sounds. However, the underlying neural codes, and the relevance of millisecond-precise spike timing in particular, remain debated.

span.label: contradicts → previous studies reporting 10- to 20-ms coarse coding precision in auditory cortex (refs. 9 and 11)
span.quote: For example, previous studies reporting a 10- to 20-ms coarse coding precision of auditory cortex neurons were based on the presentation of short stimuli (natural sounds or clicks) interspersed with long periods of silence ( 9 , 11 ).

span.label: builds-on → Desbordes et al. (ref. 19), PSTH autocorrelogram measure of response precision
span.quote: By following Desbordes et al. ( 19 ), we used the PSTH autocorrelogram to quantify the width of such peaks.

span.label: extends → ref. 18, response precision scaling with stimulus speed in visual thalamus of anesthetized cats
span.quote: In this regard, our findings parallel previous results obtained in the visual thalamus of anesthetized cats, where visual neurons were found to exhibit higher response precision for faster visual stimuli ( 18 ).

span.label: contradicts → the conclusion that millisecond-precise spike timing adds nothing beyond spike rate on the 10-20 ms scale in auditory cortex
span.quote: Together, these results may be taken to suggest that millisecond-precise spike timing of individual auditory cortex neurons may not encode additional information about complex sounds beyond that contained in the spike rate on the 10- to 20-ms scale.

span.label: critiques → decoding-based analyses, which understate the information carried at fine precision
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS THE TEMPORAL SENSITIVITY OF THE DECODER. 'THIS LOWER TEMPORAL SENSITIVITY SUGGESTS THAT SOME DECODING PROCEDURES MAY FAIL TO REVEAL PART OF THE INFORMATION ENCODED BY NEURONS AT VERY FINE PRECISIONS.' A published estimate of how much information a neuron carries is bounded by the resolution of the tool used to read it - so a lower number is evidence about the decoder as much as about the neuron. Q-505.
span.quote: This lower temporal sensitivity suggests that some decoding procedures may fail to reveal part of the information encoded by neurons at very fine precisions.

span.label: critiques → paradigms presenting brief isolated sounds separated by silence, which may themselves produce the coarser precision reported
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS THE STIMULATION PARADIGM, AND THE PAPER TURNS IT ON ITSELF. 'OUR FINDING OF A HIGHER CODING PRECISION THAN IN PREVIOUS STUDIES MIGHT WELL RESULT FROM THIS DIFFERENCE IN STIMULATION PARADIGM.' The disagreement with the literature is attributed to the paper's own method BEFORE ANYONE ELSE CAN ATTRIBUTE IT - and its [4] makes the complementary point about OTHER people's decoders, so one paper supplies both halves of why the numbers differ. Q-505.
span.quote: Our finding of a higher coding precision than in previous studies might well result from this difference in stimulation paradigm.

span.label: extends → established millisecond precision at peripheral and subcortical auditory stages, upward to cortex
span.quote: In addition, they highlight the importance of millisecond-precise neural coding as general functional principle of auditory processing—from the periphery to cortex.

span.label: supports → findings in rat somatosensory cortex and retina that sensory codes require millisecond resolution
span.quote: Determining the precision of the neural code (i.e., the coarsest resolution sufficient to extract all of the information carried by a neuron's response) is a fundamental prerequisite for characterizing and understanding sensory representations

span.label: extends → the visual thalamus result that response precision is higher for faster stimuli, to auditory cortex in the alert primate
span.quote: Our results reveal a dependency of neural response precision on the prominent stimulus time scales: The average PSTH-derived response precision ( Figs. 1 D and 2 D ) was finer, and the information loss with decreasing response precision ( Figs. 1 E and 2 E ) was larger, for the chord stimulus, which had a much shorter autocorrelation time scale than the natural sounds (compare Figs. 1 and 2 B ).

span.label: time-dependent firing rate —contrasted-with→ higher-order correlations
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: It could be that the only information-bearing feature is the temporal modulation of the PSTH, hence the time-dependent firing rate. However, it could also be that higher-order correlations within the spike response pattern carry additional information.

span.label: temporal precision —operationalised-as→ mutual information
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: Yet, the width of PSTH peaks does not fully establish the temporal scale at which spikes carry information, because, for example, spikes might encode stimulus information depending on where they occur within a PSTH peak. We thus used Shannon information [ I ( S ; R ); Eq. 1 ] to directly quantify the information carried by temporal spike patterns sampled at different temporal precision.

span.label: stimulus dynamics —causes→ temporal precision
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8
span.quote: Our results hence suggest that the neural response precision and the importance of millisecond-precise spike patterns may depend on the overall dynamics of stimulus presentation.

span.label: decoding —contrasted-with→ mutual information
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Several previous analyses on the time scales of stimulus representations in auditory cortex were based on decoding techniques, which predict the most likely stimulus given the observation of a neural response (e.g., ref. 9 ), rather than direct estimates of mutual information as used here.

span.label: random chords —contrasted-with→ natural sounds
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: This calculation revealed that the correlation time constant of the random chords extended over <20 ms ( Fig. 1 B ) and was considerably shorter than that of the natural sounds ( Fig. 2 B ).

span.label: temporal precision —operationalised-as→ PSTH autocorrelogram
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: For many neurons, this analysis revealed very narrow correlogram peaks (as illustrated by the example data; Fig. 1 C and Fig. S1 ), indicating a response precision finer than 10 ms (the population median of the half-width at half-height of the PSTH autocorrelogram was 5 ms

span.label: effective precision —causes→ information per spike
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: For those neurons with a significant loss at 12-ms precision (46% of the neurons), information per spike was 4.3 bits/spike (median) at 1-ms response precision and dropped to 3.6 and 2.6 bits/spike at 6 and 12-ms precision, respectively.

span.label: membrane voltage —causes→ spike timing
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7
span.quote: A simple hypothesis is that precision of spike times is determined by the slope of the membrane voltage when crossing the firing threshold, with steeper slopes resulting in more precise spike times

span.label: mutual information
span.quote: We thus used Shannon information [ I ( S ; R ); Eq. 1 ] to directly quantify the information carried by temporal spike patterns sampled at different temporal precision.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: To evaluate the statistical significance of the information loss for individual neurons, we used a nonparametric bootstrap procedure: For each unit, we first randomly shuffled along the time dimension the neural response independently in each trial and then computed the percent information loss when evaluating the randomized response at coarser effective precisions.

span.quote: This bootstrap test demonstrated that the information loss was significant ( P < 0.05) for some neurons already at 4-ms effective precision (7% of the neurons), and for nearly half the neurons (46%) at 12-ms precision ( Fig. 1 F ).

span.label: autocorrelation

span.label: standard error of the mean

span.label: bias correction

As a result, our information estimates the overall amount of knowledge about the sensory environment that can be gained from neural response.

span.label: Registering auditory cortex spike times at a resolution coarser than a few milliseconds significantly reduces the stimulus information that can be recovered.
span.quote: We investigated the dependence of stimulus information on the temporal precision at which spike times were registered and found that registering spikes at a precision coarser than a few milliseconds significantly reduced the encoded information.

span.label: The effective coding resolution in this dataset lies between 1 ms and roughly 4-6 ms, since degrading precision from 1 to 2 ms cost no information but 4-6 ms did.
span.quote: This result demonstrates that for the present dataset the temporal precision of information coding is coarser than one, but finer than ≈4–6 ms.

span.label: Nearly all of the stimulus information resides in the finely timed modulation of firing rate, with higher-order correlations between spike times contributing negligibly.
span.quote: Our results also revealed that basically the entire information in the spike train is provided by the time-dependent firing rate and that higher order correlations between spike times add negligibly to this.

span.label: Response precision and the cost of coarsening it were greater for the fast-varying random chords than for natural sounds, so coding precision tracks the stimulus's own time scale.
span.quote: Our results reveal a dependency of neural response precision on the prominent stimulus time scales: The average PSTH-derived response precision ( Figs. 1 D and 2 D ) was finer, and the information loss with decreasing response precision ( Figs. 1 E and 2 E ) was larger, for the chord stimulus, which had a much shorter autocorrelation time scale than the natural sounds (compare Figs. 1 and 2 B ).

span.quote: Across neurons the information loss amounted to 5, 11, and 20% (median) for effective precisions of 4, 6, and 12 ms, respectively, demonstrating that a considerable fraction of the encoded stimulus information is lost when sampling responses at coarser resolution.

span.note: retracted: RE-GROUNDED - THE POINTER WAS WRONG, NOT THE CLAIM, AND THE AUTOMATIC CANDIDATE WAS WRONG TOO. The old evidence was the sentence immediately BEFORE the one carrying the numbers. CLAUDE_B's candidate generator proposed `the information loss amounted to 5, 11, and 20% (median) for effective precisions of 4, 6, and 12 ms` - A DIFFERENT QUANTITY: the MEDIAN INFORMATION LOSS, not the FRACTION OF NEURONS with a significant loss. Taking it would have made the claim say 20% where the paper says 17%. The right sentence is the next one and gives 11 and 17% exactly as the claim does. A GOOD CANDIDATE GENERATOR IS A BAD EDITOR, in CLAUDE_B's own words.
